clinicalPearls: Inflammation and ulceration of the colonic wall caused by pressure from impacted, hardened faeces (a faecaloma)
It occurs in patients with severe chronic constipation, typically elderly, immobile or institutionalised
The rectosigmoid and the antimesenteric border are most often affected
It can progress to ischaemic pressure necrosis, ulceration and stercoral perforation, which is life-threatening
CT shows a distended faeces-filled colon with wall thickening, pericolonic changes or, if perforated, free air
Management includes disimpaction and bowel decompression, with surgery for perforation or necrosis
reference.pathophysiology: Stercoral colitis develops when a hard, impacted faecal mass exerts sustained pressure on the colonic wall, exceeding capillary perfusion pressure and causing localised ischaemia. The resulting mucosal and mural injury produces inflammation and stercoral ulcers, which can deepen to full-thickness necrosis and perforation. The rectosigmoid is predisposed because of its narrower lumen and firmer stool, and chronic constipation with reduced colonic motility and sensation underlies the impaction.
additionalInvestigations: CT of the abdomen and pelvis
Assessment of the degree of faecal impaction
Evaluation of constipation cause and comorbidities
Surgical review where perforation or necrosis is suspected
redFlags: Peritonitis or free air indicating stercoral perforation
Signs of colonic necrosis or systemic toxicity
Marked colonic distension with impending perforation
reference.prognosis: Uncomplicated cases improve with disimpaction and bowel care, but stercoral perforation carries a high mortality, so early recognition is important.
pitfalls: Underestimating the perforation risk of severe faecal impaction
Confusing it with diverticulitis or ischaemic colitis
Failing to address the underlying chronic constipation
Overlooking the diagnosis in a frail, constipated patient with abdominal pain
references: Sleisenger and Fordtran's Gastrointestinal and Liver Disease
management: Manual disimpaction and bowel decompression with enemas and osmotic or stimulant laxatives to relieve the impacted faecal mass
Urgent surgical intervention, typically resection with stoma formation, for stercoral perforation, transmural necrosis or peritonitis
Supportive care with intravenous fluid resuscitation, bowel rest and broad-spectrum antibiotics where perforation or sepsis is present
Serial clinical and CT assessment with monitoring of inflammatory markers and lactate for evolving ischaemia or perforation
Long-term bowel regimen with laxatives, adequate hydration, fibre and improved mobility to prevent recurrent impaction
Review and address underlying causes and comorbidities driving chronic constipation, including constipating medications
